attributes.body:
In a similar way to how ところ (sometimes shortened to とこ) means 'about to (A)', or 'on the verge of (A)', when following the non-past form of a verb, when following the auxiliary verb た, ところ will mean 'just did (A)'.

To use this structure, make the past tense of any verb, and then add ところ.

While this expresses 'just did (A)', ていた may be used when you would like to express that you were 'just doing (A)'.

Caution

When the kanji form of 所（ところ） is used, it is often referring to an actual physical location, rather than a situation/standpoint. However, this is something that native speakers will sometimes mistake. Therefore, seeing the kanji form and the hiragana form are both relatively common.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar
[AIAIJ] An Integrated Approach to Intermediate Japanese

attributes.body: たところだ and るところだ share the same structure, with the tense indicating whether the action is complete or not. るところだ uses the non-past form to mean 'about to do' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べるところだ ('I'm just about to eat dinner.'). たところだ uses the past form to mean 'just did' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べたところだ ('I just ate dinner.').

attributes.body: たところだ and たとたんに are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but with different usage and nuance. たところだ simply describes the timing, e.g. 家に帰ってきたところだ ('I just got home.'). In contrast, とたんに expresses that something else happened immediately at that moment. For example, 家に帰ってきたとたんに雨が降ってきた ('The instant I got home, it started to rain.').

attributes.body: たところだ and たばかり are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but with slightly different nuances. Both 晩ご飯を食べたところです and 晩ご飯を食べたばかりです essentially mean 'I just ate dinner.', but while the version with ところ focuses solely on the timing, the version with ばかり carries a nuance of continued relevance, e.g. implying '...and that's why I'm not hungry now' or '...and so I want to rest before working out'.

attributes.body: たところだ and たて are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but they differ in usage and nuance. たところだ uses the past tense of a verb and simply describes the timing, e.g. パンを焼いたところだ ('I just baked some bread.'). In contrast, たて attaches to verb stems and has the nuance of 'freshly done/finished', e.g. 焼きたてのパンが一番美味しい ('Freshly baked bread is the most delicious.').
